claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a simple, single-phase solid solution.
The single-phase solid solution is likely FCC.
Single-phase equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high plasticity or favorable machinability but low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength arise from enhanced dislocation mobility.
A nearly uniform lattice and homogeneous chemical distribution produce minimal internal barriers to dislocation motion.
The homogeneous chemical distribution produces low lattice distortion and weak solid-solution strengthening.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale, potentially Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates in the solid-solution matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitates increase lattice friction and impede plastic deformation.
Precipitate-induced obstruction of dislocation glide increases hardness and strength.
Aged specimens will have measurably higher hardness than as-quenched specimens tested under the same room-temperature conditions.
Aged specimens will have measurably higher strength than as-quenched specimens tested under the same room-temperature conditions.
After aging, nanoscale precipitates will be present within a predominantly solid-solution matrix.
High plasticity will be maintained after precipitation strengthening.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature tensile, compressive, or hardness testing.
The proposed mechanism applies only in a composition range that does not spontaneously form complex intermetallic phases.
The relevant aging regime forms nanoscale precipitates without substantially changing the alloy's overall composition.

contradictions.description: The intervention and predicted outcome require a precipitate-containing matrix, which is intrinsically a multiphase microstructure, while the boundary says aging must avoid transition into multiphase regimes.
